name: Brace
comment: Syntax highlighting for lang="brace" Vue SFC templates. Every delimiter is on its own line, so the brace rules anchor to line starts; everything else is a Vue template, included last so these rules win. The markup rules mirror the order of Vue.volar's own `html-stuff`: Vue's rules for component tags first, then `text.html.derivative`, then `text.html.basic`. Vue's rules must come first because `text.html.basic` scopes any tag whose name has no hyphen as `invalid.illegal.unrecognized-tag`, so every component would be painted with the theme's error colour. The whole `text.html.vue` grammar must NOT be included: the block rule in brace.vue-block.json is injected *into* it, so including it from here is a reference cycle and the markup loses all scoping.

brace-comment.comment: Anchored to a line start so `https://example.com` in body text stays text.

brace-for.comment: @for (item of items; index i; key item.id) { — separate from the other openers because `index` and `key` introduce clauses rather than naming variables. The clauses have a fixed order in the language, so they can be captured directly; a nested rule for the keywords did not apply inside a capture, and `index`/`key` came out highlighted as TypeScript variables.

brace-dynamic-tag.comment: <{expr}>   <{expr} attr="value" />   </{expr}>. The attributes reuse the same two rules Vue's own `tag-stuff` uses, so directives, attribute names and attribute values highlight exactly as they do on a static tag. (`tag-stuff` itself is anchored with `\G`, which does not hold inside a capture region.)

brace-expression.comment: Expressions are close enough to JS to borrow its grammar. Vue's own directive and interpolation rules scope template expressions as `source.ts#expression` (TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript, and it is what a normal template uses), so brace expressions use the same grammar instead of `source.js`. `@for` clauses (`index i`, `key x.id`) are not valid JS or TS, so they only highlight loosely.
